b:
A friend who angel invests shared that some of his pre-seed investments
are considering shutting down before even trying to raise their next round.
This isn’t super surprising; many early-stage startups are struggling to hit the growth expectations to raise,
which are extremely high at the moment, but what’s been interesting is
why these companies are losing confidence: they’re just not sure there’s a need for software anymore,
given how rapidly a good harness with a frontier model can build.
This anxiety about the future isn’t limited to young startups; you can find it in startups of almost
any size right now, boiling down to the fear that a lab might recreate your business tomorrow as a side project.

The anxiety is not purely economic.
For folks who are personally ambitious and want to have an impact
on our profession, it’s easy to feel like all work done outside of
the frontier labs is meaningless.
The tech ecosystem has always been an echo chamber,
and over the past year the participants in the echo chamber have concentrated.
It’s not just the folks who have been writing thoughtfully about LLM evolution and ecosystem
for years like Simon Willison or Claire Vo;
many leads within frontier labs have become celebrities like Boris or poteto,
and prolific authors like Addy Osmani have joined frontier labs and started publishing there.

As someone who did not join the labs when dozens of folks I previously managed did, I’ve occasionally pondered if I’ve
delivered a grave strategic wound to my own relevance, and wanted to write down my case for advancing the industry outside the labs in 2026.
I’ve been thinking about this for a few years, and parts of my thinking have endured over the last two decades,
parts have endured over the past two years, and some parts I’ve only unpacked over the past few months.

My long-term goal for my writing is to advance the industry (pt 2)
by being thoughtful, transparent, and practical.
My writing has always been an accurate reflection of my experience,
even though that’s never the best short-term strategy to increase distribution.
Sometimes that contributes to my writing being overly plain, and that’s a tradeoff I willingly make.
Nothing about the last few years has made me want to revisit this approach.
Two years: much of AI is a bubble

When I joined Imprint a couple years ago,
I enjoyed getting to know Daragh, and the impact the business was having for the companies we partnered with.
But that wasn’t my whole thesis: I also wanted to join a company whose business was growing
well, and whose economic value was not highly dependent on AI.
For short-term investors, bubbles matter because timing determines their return,
but bubbles have an inescapable impact on company culture,
even when the company is “winning.”

My professional goal at this point in my life is cultivating, and participating within, environments
where I and folks I admire are able to do the best work of our lives.
That’s hard to do! It’s even harder to do in a company that’s highly exposed to a bubble,
because tenure matters a lot when it comes to doing excellent work.
Technical context is relatively transferable, but domain context is not, and
quality is the intersection of both.
There’s a chance of doing extraordinary work in a bubble, but bubbles breed mercenary behavior, with substantial jumping across roles.
There’s nothing inherently wrong with being mercenary–which mostly means looking out for yourself–but it’s at odds with
the sort of durably excellent environment I am striving to create.
Two months: independent reproduction of results

Even if you accept my two-decade and two-year arguments, it’s still not
quite clear what the opportunity for engineers in non-labs is to shape our industry.
My take is that our biggest opportunity is to independently reproduce the stated
results from the publishing and marketing machines of the lab ecosystems.
We get to figure out what’s actually effective in a world where token spend is metered,
economic results are measured, and even the best vibes only get you to Meets Expectations.

For example, there was a period earlier this year where you were either tokenmaxing
or you were behind. But, as best I can tell, tokenmaxing was a transient meme;
instead, what mattered was ensuring everyone in your company could use a frontier model
without friction. Imprint got there without the tokenmaxing detour, instead by focusing
directly on the biggest, albeit not very exciting, blocker: addressing restrictive
financial and IT controls that prevented adoption.

That’s such an obvious point that it’s hard to even write about, because anyone who’s
thinking deeply about the problem already knows it, and anyone not thinking about the
problem will dismiss it as too banal to mention.
However, that is exactly the sort of thing we should be writing about, and the
best current opportunity to shape the industry’s current evolution.

Some of my writing along those lines this year has been
Shipping 100+ PRs to production in a week,
The Explorer Pattern for product invention and development,
and Speeding up code review with small-change.
I think this is the most interesting and impactful place to be writing right now,
and it’s only outside of a lab (away from the immense economic influences shaping narratives within labs)
that we can write about it usefully (constrained by the practical constraints experienced by
companies with things like budgets and current customers who matter at least equivalently to future customers).
